He said that the grey, and never ending snow and soot, were Fenrir, and that he ate the light. From inside, he was burnt, and now is ash that rains with the snow and cold.

Grandfather would say that many gods lived then, and walked the plains, back when they were green and good. Dhonr with his hammer that shook the earth, Udan the All Father, was a sage and seer and wise warrior. But they have all died, like that fire in the sky. But they died in battle to teach us that war has no victor - only the dead and the damned.

He was the last of the original colony left. His muscle and sinew strained under his leathery skin, his complexion uncommonly dark. I nibbled on some moss as he dragged the water-powered generator closer to the stream next to which we slept. Grandpa used to venture out into the frigid dark regularly, returning with food and goods. We were no longer able to leave our home. Rebreathers no longer functioned outside and no amount of furs and old-world jackets could shield us from the wind and ice. My father and the large group he was with were the first ones to find this out.

Grandpa supported the modest community that still remained, a small number compared to the initial group that first occupied our home. He maintained the massive garden that had been built when the ball of fire he always reminisced about first extinguished. It was my favorite area of our home, a stark contrast from the dimly lit walls where shadows danced from the small fires littered about. He ensured the UV lights in the garden were functional and that the generator was kept in working condition. It would often sputter and stop and grandpa would frantically run over to it. Grandpa was not especially talkative, but the abundance of salvaged liquor changed that every night.

“It was different back then, Aidan,” he slurred once he had reached the bottom of his bottle. "This place was just called Yellowstone," he chuckled as he reached behind his seat for another bottle. His arm seemed to disappear in the darkness. It was something to which I was still not accustomed. The rest of us were practically luminescent, easy to spot from across some of the narrower networks of the cave. He would recall so fondly the warmth he felt before what he called the “sun” died, “We weren’t confined in this prison. We could go out, we could live – well, hell, I guess we’ve always been in a type of prison. Even since before your time. We were all so focused on these trivialities that we didn’t even realize what was really happening. The whole world argued about nothing and we just-“ The generator sputtered and he groaned and stumbled towards the dying machine. These are really the only conversations that I remember with grandpa. Being that these sermons were generally delivered while he drowned himself in spirits, I couldn’t always make sense of them. With his age, the alcohol, and the creeping cold, it was not surprising that one morning, he simply didn’t wake up. Despite teaching me how to repair the generator, it died with him, completely irreparable. The lights went out, and our greenery withered.

The rest of the community did not take long to follow suit. Over just a few years, our food stockpiles slowly dwindled, the cold was relentless, but most of all, it was hard to breathe. The few children of the community were the first to go, followed by their grief-stricken parents. In the end, it was just me. I put on a few furs, and grabbed one of the remaining torches from the wall. I walked a few miles towards the entrance to the cold abyss, pushing aside or pulling down a number of tarps and furs and linens to get there. Even through the stacked stones at the end, I felt the black and chill wind engulf me. I toppled the heavy, makeshift blockade piece by piece and crawled over the pile of rocks to the outside. My first time seeing, my first time knowing, and I will soon be gone. I looked up as I felt the ice creep into my bones. A profusion of our own human crafts dotted the sky, the lights on each craft bright enough to take the place of stars. Their self-sustaining energy sources kept the occupants aboard the ships warm and well-fed. The human species would not die with me, but I began to understand what grandpa had always talked about as my eyes grew heavy.
